summary: Initial POC scoping to validate OpenAI-compatible endpoints and function calling for StrataRail. Focus: success criteria (latency/accuracy/cost), workload sizing, benchmark plan, SDK integration path, timeline for 4-week pilot.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Meyers: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna run through the POC scope for the OpenAI bridge and integration. Quick intros.
[00:18] Evelyn Park: Hi — Evelyn here, head of ML at StrataRail. We're evaluating Redwood to replace some of our homegrown inference routing. We're interested in function calling and structured outputs for manifest generation.
[00:34] Marco Ruiz: Marco, platform eng. Mainly concerned about sustained throughput and peaky loads during scheduling windows.
[00:46] Priya Nair: Priya, I'm the solutions engineer — I'll own the benchmark harness and the perf plan. Quick note, there may be slight name mismatches in the call transcripts, sorry in advance.
[01:05] Lina Chen: Lina, product. Primary success criteria: latency < 400ms p90 for 150-token responses, and extraction accuracy for structured manifests above 95% on our eval set.
[01:24] Jordan Meyers: Good, thanks. Just to set expectations — our typical POC is 3–4 weeks: week 1 infra & baseline, week 2 benchmarks, week 3 integration + tool calling, week 4 tuning and evaluation. Does that align?
[01:45] Evelyn Park: Yeah broadly. We have regulatory constraints — need audit logs retained 12 months and KMS-managed keys for any private deployment.
[02:02] Davon Holt: Davon, security — confirm SOC2 and ISO references and we need SAML SSO for console.
[02:12] Jordan Meyers: Noted — we will share SOC2 and ISO artifacts, and SAML is supported.
[02:25] Priya Nair: Ok on benchmarks — first I need workload sizing. Marco, can you share peak RPS and token distribution?
[02:36] Marco Ruiz: Sure. Normal state is ~200 RPS, peak scheduling windows up to 1,200 RPS for short bursts. Average input prompt 350 tokens, average generation 150 tokens. Concurrent connections ~5k across microservices.
[02:58] Priya Nair: Great — that's helpful. For POC we'll model a scaled-down target: sustained 250 RPS with bursts to 1k for 5 minutes to validate autoscaling and fallbacks. We'll test three model profiles: 1) base open model quantized 4-bit, 2) mid-size tuned variant, 3) Redwood-verified low-latency variant.
[03:22] Evelyn Park: Can you do token cost estimates? We care about e2e unit economics.
[03:30] Jordan Meyers: We'll provide cost per 1k tokens across those profiles. Expect quantized routes to cut inference cost by ~40% in some cases but may trade latency.
[03:44] Priya Nair: On latency SLOs — Lina mentioned 400ms p90 for 150-token responses. For the models we'll record p50/p90/p99 and tail latency during 1k-RPS bursts. We'll instrument KV cache hit rates; if prefix caching hits >30% we expect substantial tail improvement.
[04:10] Marco Ruiz: Important — we use an internal toolchain that expects OpenAI-like endpoints. We don't want to rewrite a lot of code. How compatible is Redwood's OpenAI-bridge?
[04:21] Samir Patel: Samir here — we have an OpenAI-compatible API layer that supports the typical chat/completions/embeddings surface and function calling semantics. There are a few field name differences in older SDKs but the bridge maps them. We'll provide an SDK shim if you prefer.
[04:40] Lina Chen: Function calling — we need deterministic JSON output for manifests. How do you guarantee structured output?
[04:49] Priya Nair: We support structured output via schema validation on the server side and response verification. For the POC we'll enforce JSON schema for the manifest with a schema file you provide and run an accuracy eval. If model output deviates, we fallback to a safe reject path or a simplified parser.
[05:12] Evelyn Park: What's the false positive/negative risk for schema validation?
[05:18] Priya Nair: Depends on prompt engineering and model variant. In our internal tests with similar manifest tasks, we hit ~96% pass rate after a small set of 50 targeted prompt examples. For the POC we'll do a prompt sweep.
[05:36] Jordan Meyers: Let's talk telemetry and tracing — Lina, what do you need in terms of traces?
[05:44] Lina Chen: We need per-request tracing, token-level cost breakdown, and model selection trace — basically everything you'd show in Console. Also integration with our Datadog is preferred.
[05:58] Samir Patel: We can stream events and push metrics into Datadog; we also emit structured logs for audit. Note there might be a small delay for streaming vs batch exports.
[06:12] Marco Ruiz: Network — on private deployment we need VPC peering and specific egress IPs. Can Redwood dedicate IPs?
[06:21] Jordan Meyers: Yes for Dedicated and Private, we can provide static egress ranges and VPC peering options. We'll capture exact windows for firewall changes.
[06:33] Davon Holt: KMS — we need keys in our KMS, not Redwood's.
[06:38] Priya Nair: Supported. For Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. We'll include a diagram in the security packet.
[06:48] Jordan Meyers: Back to bench plan — Priya, outline the proposed benchmark steps.
[06:55] Priya Nair: Step 0: Baseline with your sample dataset (we'll request ~500 representative prompts). Step 1: Synthetic RPS ramp (sustained 250 RPS, bursts to 1k) across three model profiles, measure p50/p90/p99 and cost. Step 2: Function-calling pass/fail rate against JSON schema + accuracy evaluation on your labeled set. Step 3: Failure mode tests — forced capacity constraints, model fallback to cheaper variant, and network egress degradation. Step 4: Integration test with your SDK against OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Timing: we expect Steps 0–2 in week 2, Step 3 in week 3, Step 4 integration in week 3.
[07:41] Marco Ruiz: For the SDK integration — do you have an official Node/Python SDK and an OpenAPI spec?
[07:48] Samir Patel: Yes, we have Node and Python SDKs; the OpenAI-compat layer exposes a swagger/openapi artifact. We'll hand you a Postman collection and a small adapter sample.
[07:58] Evelyn Park: About benchmarks — can you run the quantized models on NVidia A10s and on an x86 CPU fallback? We want to see cross-hardware behavior.
[08:08] Priya Nair: We can run on GPUs (A10s, A100 if needed) and CPU-quantized runtime for a limited set. CPU latency will be higher but important for fallback. We'll label hardware in the report.
[08:21] Lina Chen: We also need structured output to include confidence scores per field for downstream business logic.
[08:29] Priya Nair: We'll include numeric confidences and a normalized field-level confidence in the JSON output.
[08:36] Jordan Meyers: Any regulatory data residency constraints?
[08:40] Evelyn Park: All data must remain in EU for the pilot subset; global can be elsewhere.
[08:47] Jordan Meyers: We'll ensure regional routing for those requests.
[08:51] Davon Holt: Also need per-token redaction logs — we can't log full PII.
[08:56] Samir Patel: We have token-level masking and redaction hooks. For PII we'll run inline redaction or store only hashed artifacts.
[09:07] Priya Nair: Ok, one wrinkle — tool/function calling with side effects. If the model triggers manifests that create jobs in your scheduler, we'll include a dry-run mode for the POC. No writes without a confirmation callback.
[09:21] Marco Ruiz: Dry-run is required. We can't have experiments create real shipments.
[09:25] Evelyn Park: Fine. For success criteria recap: 1) p90 latency < 400ms for 150-token responses under sustained load, 2) manifest schema pass rate >95% on labeled set, 3) cost per 1M tokens within threshold (we'll evaluate), 4) reliable OpenAI-compat integration with no SDK rewrites beyond adapter.
[09:50] Jordan Meyers: Great summary. Any blockers to getting started?
[09:55] Lina Chen: We'll need legal review for data processing — can you share your standard DPA?
[10:01] Jordan Meyers: Yes we'll attach the DPA in the follow-up.
[10:06] Priya Nair: For the benchmark harness, the deliverable is a Git repo with load scripts (k6), a README, and a results template. We'll also provide a sample harness runbook.
[10:18] Marco Ruiz: Can we see a short demo of function calling before we sign off on the SOW?
[10:23] Jordan Meyers: Sure — propose a 30min demo next week; we'll do a live run with your sample prompts.
[10:30] Evelyn Park: Timeline acceptance — let's target pilot kickoff 2027-03-22. Is that realistic?
[10:35] Jordan Meyers: Yes, with documents and samples in this week it's doable.
[10:40] Davon Holt: I'll need an initial sec architecture diagram for review by 2027-03-16.
[10:45] Samir Patel: We'll include that in the shared folder.
[10:50] Priya Nair: Perf metrics we'll record: tokens/sec, p50/p90/p99, cache hit rate, model-switch counts, autoscale latency, and cost per million tokens.
[11:02] Lina Chen: For evaluation, we'll do a blind scoring on a holdout set and we'll expect a joint review at the end of week 4.
[11:12] Jordan Meyers: Ok let's wrap with explicit next steps — Jordan to send SOW and pricing, Priya to upload harness, Evelyn to share sample prompts and redaction rules, Marco to confirm peering windows, Davon to review security diagram. Any final clarifications?
[11:30] Evelyn Park: One more — can you include a fallback policy spec for region failure? We need concrete behavior.
[11:37] Priya Nair: We'll add fallback policy: route to secondary region model variant, degrade to smaller model variant, or return a queued response depending on SLA preference. We'll document priorities.
[11:50] Jordan Meyers: Thanks everyone. We'll send notes and links after the call.
[12:00] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript contains occasional misheard product names and rapid speech. Links referenced: benchmark harness (to be shared), SOW draft (to be shared), security pack (to be shared).
